stemMd:
> Since the city introduced its requirement that every rental contract be registered electronically, the number of disputes brought before the rent tribunal has fallen by a third. The requirement is therefore producing better-drafted contracts.

The argument depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Electronic registration costs landlords less than the paper procedure it replaced.

options.label: B
options.textMd: The fall in disputes is not explained by tenants having become less willing or less able to bring a claim.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Every rental contract concluded in the city is now registered electronically.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Rent tribunals in other cities have not recorded a comparable fall over the same period.

explanationMd:
Separate what is observed from what is inferred. **Observed:** fewer disputes reach the tribunal. **Inferred:** contracts are better drafted. The inference reads a drop in *filed disputes* as a drop in *dispute-worthy contracts*.

That step only works if nothing else has reduced filings. If tenants have become less willing to go to the tribunal — a higher fee, a longer wait, worse advice — filings would fall while the contracts stayed exactly as bad as before. Option B rules that rival explanation out, so the argument depends on it.

**How to check — the negation test.** Negate the candidate and see whether the argument still stands. Negate B: *the fall is explained by tenants having become less willing or able to claim.* The conclusion collapses at once, because the evidence would then be about tenant behaviour rather than contract quality. Negate any other option and the argument still stands: it survives registration being more expensive, it survives a few unregistered contracts, and it survives other cities falling too, even though that last one makes it less persuasive. Only B fails the test, which is what makes it the assumption.

distractorRationale.a: Cost to landlords is beside the point. The argument is about the quality of drafting and the number of disputes, and it would run identically if electronic registration were the more expensive option, so this is not something the argument needs.
distractorRationale.c: Universal compliance is more than the argument requires. A requirement that raised drafting standards across most contracts would explain a one-third fall perfectly well, so the argument survives the negation of this option and does not rest on it.
distractorRationale.d: A comparison with other cities would help *confirm* the argument by ruling out a nationwide cause, which makes it useful supporting evidence rather than an assumption. The argument as stated never appeals to other cities, and negating this option leaves its reasoning intact even if it becomes less persuasive.

accessibilityText: A verbal reasoning question. A short argument states that since a city required rental contracts to be registered electronically, disputes before the rent tribunal have fallen by a third, and concludes that the requirement is producing better-drafted contracts. The question asks which of four statements is an assumption the argument depends on.

provenance.notes: Original argument-analysis item written to the published Bocconi Law syllabus entry 'identifying the assumption on which an argument depends'. The city, policy and figures are invented.

review.author: bocconi-law-wave3-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: The argument infers better drafting from fewer disputes, so it must assume the fall is not explained by tenants being less willing or able to claim. If (b) is negated, the conclusion collapses. (a) is irrelevant to contract quality. (c) is stronger than the argument needs. (d) would support the argument but is not required, because a comparable fall elsewhere would not by itself defeat it.

review.notes: Author applied the negation test to all four options. Only B destroys the argument when negated: a fall caused by reduced claiming leaves contract quality untouched. A is irrelevant, C is stronger than needed, D would strengthen the argument but is not required by it. Correction by the coordinating editor (an AI agent); a separate AI reviewer then re-checked every claim about the options, and the item passed a new blind solve on 2026-09-24. v1 stays attached to earlier attempts.
